status: wired (2026-07-26): AgentSpec logic lives in the shared core public/js/agent-spec-core.js (server façade src/agent-spec.js; sdk/pair-cli.mjs re-exports it); the Agent Studio mode and share-link minting resolve agents from this file via the committed source snapshot. An agent is DEFINED by its chat-input-pane controls, its intro + loading animations, its colour theme, its seed example questions, the default quota a minted share-link token carries, and — since 0.2.0 — its CAPABILITY block. Derive a new agent by copying one of these and changing those fields.
capability_note: The `capability` block (0.2.0) is a SELECTOR over behaviour the platform already implements, never a place to define new behaviour: every value is a member of a closed vocabulary that names existing code. That is what keeps invariant 1 (deterministic orchestration, no function calling) intact — the dispatch stays code, the spec is data read before the run starts. Validation enforces invariant 3 (planning phases stay on the fixed JSON model), invariant 4 (a client-tier agent may not select anything that puts the server in the data path) and invariant 6 (a declared gate routes Swedish and English alike).
executed_note: Since 2026-07-26 the block is EXECUTED, not only declared. `bounds`, `tools`, `search` and (since 2026-08-13) `context` are read off the resolved capability at run start through four NARROWING accessors — capBound / capSearch / capHasTool / capHasContext — each of which takes the platform's own limit as BOTH the default and the ceiling. An absent, malformed or over-large declaration all resolve to the platform's value, so no declaration can reach further than the code already reaches: the worst a hostile capability block can do is make its own agent do less. One rule to know: a capability governs the phase it NAMES and no other, which is why introspection's `search.web: false` does not follow a turn the external-source gate handed back to research. `context` became EXECUTED on 2026-08-13: capHasContext gates the enrichment registry (src/enrichment.js), the extension registry (src/extensions.js) and the search-source registry's `requiresContext` (src/search-sources.js), so a retrieval block runs only for an agent that declared it. One asymmetry is deliberate: a NULL capability means no agent was resolved at all, so it keeps every search source rather than none. `gates`, `emits` and `team` are still declared-and-pinned rather than read.
reachability_note: An agent is reachable three ways, tried most specific first, all applying the same requirement gate: an inline `agent_spec` object on the /api/chat request (a spec the caller wrote — no registry load), an `agent` id addressing an entry in this file (no `defaults` row, flag, chat mode or CSS needed), and the `defaults` table's mode flags. Falling through is the only failure mode: an unknown id, an ungranted one and a refused inline spec all resolve to the agent the request would have got anyway, so nothing errors, nothing escalates, and probing reveals nothing.
untrusted_spec_note: A spec that did NOT come from this committed file is resolved through resolveUntrustedAgent(spec, granted), which fails closed — not an object, any validation problem, or any ungranted requirement yields no agent and the reasons why, never a partial capability. Requirements are DERIVED from what a capability selects (requirementsFor over IMPLIED_REQUIREMENTS, pinned against this registry), never read from the self-declared `requires`: a spec claiming to need nothing while selecting the build tools is refused exactly as if it had been honest. Nothing new is enforced there — the closed vocabularies, invariants 1/3/4/6 and the narrowing accessors already do the work; the boundary runs them on the request path and refuses.
agents_are_not_chat_modes: The entries below are reference AgentSpecs — templates you copy to define a new agent. They are not themselves the chat-mode dropdown, and they are not the tiers. SEVEN of them are the DEFAULT agent of a chat mode, bound to it by the `defaults` table above; two (secure, under-construction) are tier archetypes bound to no mode, and one (palaeogenomics) is a domain agent reachable by id alone. An agent PICKS a tier via `platform` (client = Se/cure, server = Se/rver) and a mode via `mode`; Secure is simply the reference agent for the client tier, not the tier itself. `derivesFrom` names the ancestor a spec was copied from: everything used to point at `research`, the general agent, and since its retirement (2026-08-13) the server-tier specs point at `baseplate` directly — there is no general agent left to inherit from, which is the whole point. Since spec 0.2.0 an agent also picks an ANSWER PHASE via `capability.answerPhase` — one of the phases the platform already implements. A spec can therefore reach any shipped execution semantics, but it still cannot invent new ones: a genuinely new executor is a row in src/pipeline.js ANSWER_PHASE_RUNNERS, written by hand.
starters_note: The `examples` field on each agent below is the SEED set — three or so questions used by Agent Studio previews and by exampleGenPrompt when generating more. It is NOT what a visitor sees on an empty chat. That is the STARTER QUEUE: a separate, deeper registry (public/js/starters-data.js, logic in public/js/starters-core.js, façade src/starters.js) holding 20+ opening questions per agent, of which four are shown at a time and rotated. The two are kept apart deliberately — a spec's examples describe the agent for someone deriving a new one, while a starter queue is a ranked, evaluated product surface whose entries carry scores from tests/starter-eval.mjs. See the **starter-prompts** skill.

control_types.depth-slider: research depth → number of pipeline search rounds
control_types.toggle: a boolean request flag (web search, incognito, …) — id IS the flag
control_types.mode-select: choose the chat mode — the app's seven canonical ids: science (Deep Science, the default) / cyber (Cyber) / introspection / sdk (Agent Studio; the spec's historical alias agent-builder still resolves to it) / orchestrator / outrospection / models (Models). The retired id `normal` (Deep Research) resolves to `science`.

defaults_note: The Se/rver app's seven DEFAULT agents — one per chat mode (public/js/chat-mode-core.js CHAT_MODES). ARRAY ORDER IS PRECEDENCE, mirroring src/chat.js: a request carrying several mode flags resolves to the first match (sdk > orchestrator > outrospection > models > introspection > cyber > science). `flag` names the /api/chat request field that selects the mode; a request may instead name its mode outright with the `chat_mode` field, which is the preferred form and what the app sends — the per-mode booleans are the legacy spelling. Until 2026-07-26 introspection had NO flag and was the derived leftover (whatever remained when the developer_mode knob was on and no other flag matched); it now has `introspection_mode` like every sibling, and `developer_mode` is an AVAILABILITY grant only, never a mode selector. Agents NOT listed here (secure, under-construction, palaeogenomics) are tier archetypes, templates and by-id domain agents, not chat modes. THE ROSTER IS SPECIFIC AND HAS NO GENERAL MEMBER (owner directive, 2026-08-13): the `normal` mode and its `research` agent — the catch-all labeled Deep Research, defined by what it did not specialise in — are gone, and `science` took the terminal-fallback slot. Two consequences follow and are load-bearing. First, the fallback agent must be reachable by ANY caller, so `scholar` alone among the mode defaults declares no `developer_mode` requirement: a requirement on the terminal row would fall through to nothing, and nothing resolves to a null capability, which is the unrestricted platform default — the exact opposite of what a fallback should be. Second, an unrouted request now gets a POLICY: Deep Science LEADS with the peer-reviewed record, which is absorbed first and so takes the first numbered sources; since 2026-08-14 (feedback #69) a knob-gated web leg runs BEHIND it, stamped as not peer-reviewed (`state.webAfterAux` / `state.webSourceNote`) and barred from standing in for the literature on a scientific claim. Before that its `search.web: false` made it structurally webless. `cyber` was added the same day as the second domain mode (after `science`, 2026-07-31), and like `science` it does not carry this site's own source.

agents.name: Secure
agents.tagline: The never-cloud tier — the research assistant that runs wholly in your browser. DeepResearch.Se/cure.
agents.description: The client tier: the server is in no data path. Provider calls go browser-direct on your own keys (or your local model server), the pipeline runs in the page, and all state rests sealed in browser-local storage. Its privacy is structural.

controls.placeholder: Ask — nothing leaves this device except the model call…

examples: Draft a privacy policy for a browser-only app that never sees my data.
Explain how AES-GCM sealing of local chat history works.
What can a static host observe about my session? What can't it?

quota.note: No server quota by default — Se/cure runs on your own keys. A share link may add a bounded, disclosed web-search grant.

agents.name: Under Construction
agents.tagline: A placeholder tier — the template you copy to start a brand-new agent.
agents.description: The minimal viable agent: a composer, a send button, and an honest 'not built yet' notice. It exists to be copied — change the name, add controls, pick a theme, and you have a new agent.
examples: What will this agent do?

quota.note: A cautious default for a work-in-progress share link.

agents.name: Introspection
agents.tagline: The site read from the inside — answers from its own deployed source and docs.
agents.description: The chat mode that investigates THIS site's implementation. The deployed source snapshot and the docs corpus are retrieved into context, then the answer model reads the real files — natively with grep_source / read_file / list_files where the model supports tool use, otherwise through the deterministic JSON read loop. Web search stays off unless the bilingual external-source gate hands the turn back to research.

controls.placeholder: Ask how this site is built…

examples: How does the deterministic research pipeline route models between phases?
Hur fungerar krypteringen av chatthistoriken i den här appen?
Assess this project's security posture from its actual source.

quota.note: Reading the snapshot is cheap; the tool loop is not — a moderate default.

agents.name: Orchestrator
agents.tagline: A team of sub-agents working in concert — planned, run in waves, merged into one answer.
agents.description: One JSON plan phase on the fixed planning model decomposes the request into a small DAG of sub-agents; the Worker executes them in parallel waves and streams a single merged answer. The plan is data and the executor is code, so no model decides control flow mid-run. A failed node degrades to an honest gap note.

controls.placeholder: Describe a task for a team of agents…

examples: Compare three vector databases: one agent per product, then merge the verdict.
Research the market, the tech and the regulation of home battery storage in Sweden.
Assess this site's privacy posture from the source and from what competitors claim.

quota.note: One request runs a whole team — a tighter default than single-agent modes.

agents.name: Outrospection
agents.tagline: Introspection's mirror image — what everyone ELSE shipped.
agents.description: The outward feed: seven standing lenses, each with its own searches, refreshed offline and on visit. A question is routed to a lens by the bilingual deterministic gate and answered from the feed's collected items. No web search runs on the turn itself, and an empty feed answers honestly rather than inventing an item.

controls.placeholder: Ask what the rest of the field shipped…

examples: What did the other deep-research products ship this month?
Vad har hänt med öppna vikter den senaste tiden?
Which privacy-first assistants launched recently, and what do they actually promise?

quota.note: Answering from a pre-collected feed is cheap — no live search on the turn.

agents.name: Models
agents.tagline: The agent whose subject is the models themselves — explore every provider, evaluate, enable.
agents.description: The model lifecycle, in one place. It researches the model landscape with the Hugging Face Hub in every search wave, and it holds the live catalog of every model this deployment can reach — Berget, Anthropic, OpenAI and the open Hugging Face router — with each one's price and its verification checklist. A model moves discovered -> evaluated -> enabled here: the checks are real probes run against the real provider dispatch, they are evidence rather than gates (a failing check is a known limitation, never a ban), and enabling puts a model in every other agent's dropdown, bounded by a starting model allowance the site config raises.

controls.placeholder: Ask about a model — which to run, what it costs, what it passed…

examples: Which model can I run here that reads images, and what does one research turn cost?
Vilken modell ska jag aktivera för svensk text, och vad har den verifierats för?
Compare the models I have enabled on price, context length and which checks they pass.

quota.note: Signed-in default window; an enabled open-catalog model bills at its own published rate, and a verification run bills like any other model call.

agents.name: lypning
agents.tagline: The measurements of one external project, and nothing else. It holds two kinds of number — what your own browser's Linux VM measured just now, and what each lypning commit published about itself — and it never lets one stand in for the other.
agents.description: A stats agent for github.com/kristerhedfors/lypning, the mixture of Pythons the execution sandbox runs: a Rust subset, a MicroPython variant with a frozen stdlib, and CPython, with a classifier that picks per program and a refusal contract (exit 90, one line on stderr, nothing on stdout) that makes a wrong pick cost one wasted spawn instead of a wrong answer. Its home is the /lypning/ dashboard, where the live half of its data comes from: the visitor's own browser Linux VM runs the battery and the agent is handed the result. Everything it says traces to one of two places and is labelled with which — COUNTED, meaning this site counted it out of the lypning tree at that commit (corpus entries, Rust lines, frozen stdlib modules), or QUOTED, meaning some commit's README published it after a run on the author's machine on a day that is gone. That distinction is not decoration: lypning's own third invariant is that a remembered corpus size is never quoted as a measurement, because every tool over there prints the count it loaded precisely because yours will differ. So this agent will say 'the mixture cost 0.302x on the author's machine at d0e7f6f, and your VM has not run the battery' rather than answering as if the two were the same claim. It searches nothing: there is no web leg and no literature leg, because the question 'how fast is this interpreter' is not answered by reading about it. When the dataset cannot be loaded it says so rather than recalling figures.
examples: How did the corpus grow?
What happened to the mixture cost ratio, and on whose machine?
Are there MISMATCHes, and whose are they?
Hur stor är binären, och hur har den ändrats?
What does my own VM measure, and how does it compare?

controls.placeholder: Ask about a measurement — what moved, when, and who measured it…

agents.name: Agent Studio
agents.tagline: The mode that builds agents — distil this site into a new flavour and publish it live.
agents.description: Formerly 'SDK mode'. Describe a flavour to distil from the Se/cure tier; the model plans against the DistillSDK manifest, reads the deployed source, builds a self-contained agent, and publishes it at /app/<slug>/. This is the pair-studio module made real.
examples: Build a single-purpose legal-research agent themed in deep blue.
Distil a stripped-down single-file Se/cure client with only a model picker.
Make a Swedish-language study assistant with a depth slider and no web search.

quota.note: Building is expensive; a share link to a builder gets a tighter default.

agents.name: Palaeogenomics
agents.tagline: Ancient DNA research: the published literature and the published individuals, kept apart.
agents.description: A research agent for ancient genetics — palaeogenomics, archaeogenetics, ancient metagenomics. It answers from two sources the plain Deep Research turn cannot reach. The literature leg searches Europe PMC (PubMed, PubMed Central, bioRxiv and medRxiv), where this field actually publishes and arXiv does not. The sample leg runs a STRUCTURED query over 20,927 published ancient and present-day individuals repackaged from the Allen Ancient DNA Resource through the Poseidon archives — a region and radius, a date window in BP/BCE/CE, an mtDNA or Y-haplogroup prefix, a coverage floor — and folds the exact matching rows and counts into the answer, so a sample id in the answer is a sample that exists. It excludes Ignore_-flagged individuals by default (the convention for contaminated, duplicated and unusable samples) and says so. Neither leg infers ancestry: the corpus query is filters and counts, not f-statistics, qpAdm or PCA — for those, the analysis belongs in the execution sandbox with the real tools. Its subject matter carries caveats that decide whether a claim holds — coverage, contamination, calibrated versus contextual dates, reference panel — and the agent is built to state them rather than round them away.

controls.placeholder: Ask about ancient DNA — a population, a site, a haplogroup, a date range…

examples: Which published ancient individuals lie within 300 km of Gotland and date between 5000 and 4000 BP?
Hur många forntida individer i databasen har Y-haplogrupp R1b, och var kommer de ifrån?
What do the papers say about DNA preservation in permafrost, and how old is the oldest sequenced mammoth?
Compare the coverage and dating evidence behind the Yamnaya samples in the corpus.

quota.note: Signed-in default window. The sample query costs no upstream call at all — the corpus is a build artifact in this deployment — so only the literature leg and the answer model bill.

agents.name: Cyber
agents.tagline: Security and OSINT. What is exposed, who runs it, what it looks like from outside.
agents.description: The cybersecurity and open-source-intelligence agent. It is the one agent that may reach the outward-facing intelligence this platform can gather: host intelligence for a hostname, IP or organization named in the conversation — open ports, running services, hosting organization and ASN, known CVEs; street-level imagery and place resolution for an address, a photo's coordinates or a panorama, which is geospatial reconnaissance rather than tourism; the OWASP Top 10 for web and for LLM applications, retrieved as real reference text for an assessment ask; and the two OSINT METHODS — the subject-disambiguation rule that refuses to merge four organisations sharing a name into one confident dossier, and the depth-scaled report scaffold whose deepest tier is shaped like a TIBER-EU targeted threat-intelligence report with its threat scenarios mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Three things it states rather than hides. It reports on what is PUBLIC: it reads what the internet already publishes, and it neither scans, probes, nor buys data — an answer that reads like an engagement report is still a desk study, and it says so. It obeys the same privacy rail every agent on this platform obeys, which bounds research about a named person to the public professional record and refuses the special categories outright — being the security agent widens what it may look up, never who it may look up. And exposure is not vulnerability: an open port is an observation, and the answer separates what was observed from what was inferred.

controls.placeholder: Name a host, a domain, an organisation or a place…

examples: What services and known CVEs does the host I name expose, and which of them are actually reachable?
Gör en OSINT-genomgång av ett svenskt bolag jag namnger — domäner, tjänster och digitalt fotavtryck.
Walk the OWASP Top 10 for a web app that stores uploads in object storage and renders them back.
What is at this address, and what does the street-level imagery show about physical access?

quota.note: Signed-in default window. The host-intelligence and street-imagery legs are metered by their own extension knobs and billed to the deployment's keys, so a share link that mints this agent still cannot spend them without the knob.

agents.name: Deep Science
agents.tagline: Peer-reviewed evidence first, then the open record to check it against. The literature leads and is numbered first; web results arrive labelled as web results — preprints only when you name the preprint record, and labelled as preprints when they arrive.
agents.description: A research agent whose evidence is the peer-reviewed literature, checked against the open record. The peer-reviewed leg LEADS every turn and is absorbed first, so the reviewed record occupies the first numbered sources; the web leg then runs behind it, and only when the reader's web-search knob is on. Its results arrive stamped as web results — not peer-reviewed, there to corroborate, date and contextualise (a retraction notice, an investigation, a citation analysis, who reported what and when), never to settle a scientific claim the reviewed literature has not settled. Before 2026-08-14 the web leg was off structurally and the agent answered from the literature alone; that changed on a reader's report (feedback #69) that the one question only the open record can answer — what a retracted paper claimed and how much later work rests on it — was the one it could not touch. The literature half is unchanged and still restricted to one source: a peer-reviewed literature search that merges OpenAlex, Europe PMC's peer-reviewed slice, Semantic Scholar, this site's own hosted PubMed index (searched by meaning, with no outbound request) and, where a licensed key is configured, Google Scholar's own ranking, then keeps only records carrying POSITIVE evidence of peer review (a journal venue with an ISSN, a Crossref journal-article, a MEDLINE/PMC indexing) and drops everything else, retractions and preprints included. It integrates with Google Scholar as far as Google permits: Scholar's robots.txt disallows the search results and explicitly allows the author profile and publication-metrics pages, so this agent reads the allowed ones — an author's Scholar h-index, i10-index and most-cited works from a profile link, and every citation's venue annotated with Google Scholar's h5-index from a committed metrics table. It never scrapes the disallowed search index. Two consequences it states rather than hides: 'from Google Scholar' and 'peer-reviewed only' are different requests, and where they conflict this agent obeys the second; and a peer-reviewed source is a reviewed source, not a correct one, so the answer reports what the literature found, in whose journal, cited how often, and where the studies disagree. Since the roster became specific (2026-08-13) this agent is also the sole OWNER of the site's two preprint-bearing corpora — arXiv and the hosted PubMed index — which no other agent can reach at all. Owning them changes what it can be asked for, not what it does by default: an ordinary turn is still the peer-reviewed leg alone, and preprints enter only when the reader names that record outright ("arxiv", "preprint", "förhandstryck", "pubmed", "bioRxiv"). Asking a research question the archives happen to serve is not naming them, so "what does the latest research say" reaches the reviewed literature and nothing else. When a preprint does arrive it is marked one in the material the model reads — every arXiv item leads with "Preprint, not peer-reviewed" and Europe PMC annotates its bioRxiv/medRxiv records the same way — so an answer covering both records cannot quietly present an unreviewed paper as a reviewed one. Retractions are the second thing that changed with #69, and in the same narrow shape as preprints: a retracted paper is still dropped on sight from an ordinary research question — cited as current evidence it is the worst failure this agent can produce — but when the reader asks about retraction, withdrawal or research misconduct outright (EN + SV), the retracted record is admitted and every such source leads with RETRACTED, so the answer reports what the paper claimed and what became of it rather than what is known. The refusals that remain: no scraping of Google Scholar's disallowed search index, no preprint unless it was asked for, no retracted paper unless the question is about retraction, and no web source standing in for peer-reviewed evidence.

controls.placeholder: Ask a question the published literature can answer…

examples: Does vitamin D supplementation reduce the risk of acute respiratory infection?
Vad säger den sakkunniggranskade forskningen om intermittent fasta och insulinkänslighet?
Which journals publish the highest-cited work in computer security, by Scholar h5-index?
Summarise this researcher's most-cited work: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=JicYPdAAAAAJ

quota.note: Signed-in default window. The literature backends are free or key-gated per deployment rather than billed per user, and no web search runs at all — so only the answer model bills.
